column4: The redesign sandbox and design system routes are publicly served with nothing preventing indexing
column5: Requested against a running dev server /redesign/ and /redesign/pdp/ and /design-system/ all return HTTP 200 and none of them emits a robots meta tag - grepping the served HTML for a robots meta returns nothing on all three. public/robots.txt contains no Disallow entry matching either path so they fall under the blanket Allow: / at the top of the file. Absence of a robots meta means indexable by default. These routes render the sandbox mock data from src/redesign/data/mock.ts rather than live catalogue data and there are 22 of them under src/pages/redesign plus the design system page.
column9: Any production deployment - the sandbox ships in the same build as the storefront.
column10: 1. Request /redesign/ and /redesign/pdp/ and /design-system/. 2. Read the HTTP status and search the response for a robots meta tag. 3. Check public/robots.txt for a matching Disallow.
column11: Internal design routes are excluded from indexing by a noindex meta or a robots.txt Disallow or by not shipping in a production build at all.
column12: All three are served with no robots restriction of any kind.
column13: Search engines can index 23 internal pages carrying placeholder copy and mock product data. They compete with real category and product pages for the same terms and publicly expose unreleased design work. Any that mirror a live screen create genuine duplicate content against the page they were built to replace.
column14: Add Disallow entries for /redesign/ and /design-system/ to the robots.txt template that scripts/update-robots.mjs consumes and emit a noindex meta on those routes. The stronger fix is to exclude the sandbox from production builds so the routes do not exist outside development.

column4: The generated sitemap advertises two routes that return 404
column5: Requested against a running dev server /delivery-zones/ returns 404 and /products/ returns 404 - and both are listed as static routes in the sitemap generator at scripts/generate-sitemap.mjs:18 and :20 with priorities 0.6 and 0.9 respectively. The sitemap is regenerated during npm run build and its location is advertised through the Sitemap directive in robots.txt. /delivery-zones/ has no page directory at all and CLAUDE.md section 9.11 states the feature is deprecated product wide and must not be ported - so the sitemap is advertising a removed feature. /products/ has no index page either since src/pages/products contains only the [slug] detail route and the search route. The other eleven static entries were checked against the filesystem and all resolve.
column9: Any production build - the sitemap is generated during npm run build.
column10: 1. Run npm run build to regenerate public/sitemap.xml. 2. Read the entries for /delivery-zones/ and /products/. 3. Request both URLs and observe a 404.
column11: Every URL in the sitemap resolves - a sitemap is a statement that these URLs are canonical and worth crawling.
column12: Two of the thirteen static entries return 404 including the one given the highest priority of any catalogue URL.
column13: Crawl budget is spent on URLs that cannot resolve and repeated 404s from a submitted sitemap reduce the trust search engines place in the whole file. Advertising the deprecated delivery-zones path also contradicts an explicit project rule.
column14: Remove both entries. Better - derive the static route list from the pages directory during generation so it cannot drift again - and add a build time assertion that every sitemap URL resolves.

column4: Every canonical URL omits the trailing slash the site actually serves so it points at a redirect
column5: next.config.ts sets trailingSlash true so the storefront serves /about-us/ and answers 308 for /about-us. The canonical tag emitted on that page is <link rel="canonical" href="http://localhost:3002/about-us"> - without the trailing slash. Verified against a running dev server: the canonical target /about-us returns 308 while the served URL /about-us/ returns 200. So the canonical points at a URL that redirects rather than at the final address of the page. The canonical value is built by getCanonicalUrl from the path passed by each page - for example canonical={`/products/${initialProduct.slug}`} at src/pages/products/[slug]/index.tsx:166 - and none of those paths carries a trailing slash.
column9: Any page that emits a canonical tag - which is 31 of the 35 non sandbox pages.
column10: 1. Open any content page such as /about-us/. 2. Read the canonical link in the head. 3. Request the canonical target and observe a 308 to the slashed form.
column11: The canonical names the exact URL the site serves - with the trailing slash - so it does not redirect.
column12: Every canonical points one redirect away from the real page.
column13: Search engines are told the canonical address of every page is a URL that immediately redirects which weakens consolidation of ranking signals and wastes crawl budget on an extra hop per page. It also disagrees with the sitemap whose entries do carry trailing slashes so the two signals conflict.
column14: Append the trailing slash in getCanonicalUrl when trailingSlash is enabled - one change covers every page - and confirm the result matches the sitemap form so the two agree.
